title: No. 76 — The Appointing Power of the Executive (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The President is "to nominate, and, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, judges of the Supreme Court, and all other officers of the United States whose appointments are not otherwise provided for in the Constitution. But the Congress may by law vest the appointment of such inferior officers as they think proper, in the President alone, in the courts of law, or in the heads of departments. The President shall have power to fill up all vacancies which may happen during the recess of the Senate, by granting commissions which shall expire at the end of their next session."

It has been observed in a former paper that "the true test of a good government is its aptitude and tendency to produce a good administration." If the justness of this observation is admitted, the mode of appointing the officers of the United States contained in the foregoing clauses must, when examined, be entitled to particular commendation. It is not easy to conceive a plan better calculated than this to promote a judicious choice of men for filling the offices of the Union. And it needs no proof that the character of its administration must essentially depend on this point.

It will be agreed on all hands that the appointing power, in ordinary cases, ought to be modified in one of three ways. It ought to be vested either in a single man, in a select assembly of moderate size, or in a single man with the concurrence of such an assembly. Its exercise by the people at large will readily be admitted impracticable; setting every other consideration aside, it would leave them little time to do anything else. So when mention is made in the following reasoning of an assembly or body of men, it must be understood to refer to a select body or assembly as already described. The people collectively, by their numbers and their dispersed location, cannot be governed in their movements by that systematic spirit of cabal and intrigue that will be urged as the chief objection to placing this power in a body of men.

Those who have themselves reflected on the subject, or who have attended to the observations made in other parts of these papers concerning the appointment of the President, will, I presume, agree to the proposition that there would always be a great probability of having the place filled by a man of abilities at least respectable. Granting this, I proceed to lay it down as a rule that one man of discernment is better fitted to analyze and assess the particular qualities suited to particular offices than a body of men of equal or perhaps even superior discernment.

The sole and undivided responsibility of one man will naturally produce a livelier sense of duty and a more exact regard to reputation. He will, on this account, feel under stronger obligations and more interested in carefully investigating the qualities required for the stations to be filled, and in impartially preferring the persons who have the fairest claims. He will have fewer personal attachments to gratify than a body of men who may each be supposed to have an equal number, and so much the less liable to be misled by sentiments of friendship and affection. A single, well-directed mind cannot be distracted and warped by that diversity of views, feelings, and interests that frequently distracts and warps the resolutions of a collective body. Nothing is so apt to stir the passions of mankind as personal considerations — whether they relate to ourselves or to others who are to be the objects of our choice or preference. Hence, in every exercise of the appointing power by an assembly of men, we must expect to see a full display of all the private and party likings and dislikes, partialities and antipathies, attachments and animosities felt by those composing the assembly. The choice that may at any time be made under such circumstances will of course be the result either of a victory by one party over the other, or of a compromise between the parties. In either case, the intrinsic merit of the candidate will too often be out of sight. In the first, the qualifications best suited to uniting the votes of the party will be more considered than those that fit the person for the station. In the second, the coalition will commonly turn on some interested equivalent: "Give us the man we want for this office, and you shall have the one you want for that." This will be the usual condition of the bargain. And it will rarely happen that advancing the public service is the primary object of either party victories or party negotiations.

The truth of the principles here advanced seems to have been felt by the most intelligent of those who have found fault with the provision the convention has made on this subject. They contend that the President alone should have been authorized to make appointments under the federal government. But it is easy to show that every advantage to be expected from such an arrangement would, in substance, be derived from the power of nomination, which is proposed to be conferred on him, while several disadvantages that might attend an absolute appointing power in his hands would be avoided. In the act of nomination, his judgment alone would be exercised. And since it would be his sole duty to point out the man who, with the Senate's approval, should fill an office, his responsibility would be as complete as if he made the final appointment. In this view, there can be no difference between nominating and appointing. The same motives that would lead to a proper discharge of his duty in one case would exist in the other. And since no man could be appointed except on his previous nomination, every man who might be appointed would in fact be his choice.

But might not his nomination be overruled? I grant it might. Yet this could only be to make room for another nomination by him. The person ultimately appointed must still be the object of his preference, though perhaps not the first. Nor is it very probable that his nomination would often be overruled. The Senate could not be tempted, by a preference they might feel for someone else, to reject the one proposed, because they could not be sure that the person they wished for would be brought forward by a second or any subsequent nomination. They could not even be certain that a future nomination would present a candidate any more acceptable to them. And since their dissent might cast a kind of stigma on the individual rejected and might appear to be a reflection on the judgment of the chief magistrate, it is unlikely that their sanction would often be refused without special and strong reasons for refusal.

To what purpose, then, require the cooperation of the Senate? I answer that the necessity of their concurrence would have a powerful, though generally silent, effect. It would be an excellent check on a spirit of favoritism in the President, and would tend greatly to prevent the appointment of unfit characters from state prejudice, family connection, personal attachment, or a view to popularity. In addition, it would be an effective source of stability in the administration.

It will be easily understood that a man who had sole control over offices would be governed far more by his private inclinations and interests than when he was bound to submit the propriety of his choice to the discussion and decision of a different and independent body — and that body an entire branch of the legislature. The possibility of rejection would be a strong motive for care in proposing. The danger to his own reputation — and, in the case of an elective magistrate, to his political existence — from betraying a spirit of favoritism, or an unbecoming pursuit of popularity, before the observation of a body whose opinion would carry great weight in forming public opinion, could not fail to act as a barrier against both. He would be both ashamed and afraid to bring forward, for the most distinguished or lucrative stations, candidates whose only merit was that of coming from the same state to which he particularly belonged, of being personally allied to him in some way, or of possessing the necessary insignificance and pliancy to render them the obsequious instruments of his pleasure.

To this reasoning it has been objected that the President, by the influence of the power of nomination, may secure the compliance of the Senate to his views. This supposition of universal venality in human nature is little less an error in political reasoning than the supposition of universal rectitude. The institution of delegated power implies that there is a portion of virtue and honor among mankind that may be a reasonable foundation of confidence — and experience justifies the theory. It has been found to exist in the most corrupt periods of the most corrupt governments. The venality of the British House of Commons has long been a topic of accusation against that body, both in the country to which they belong and here. It cannot be doubted that the charge is, to a considerable extent, well founded. But it is as little to be doubted that there is always a large proportion of the body consisting of independent and public-spirited men who carry influential weight in the councils of the nation. It is for this reason (the present reign not excepted) that the sense of that body is often seen to control the inclinations of the monarch, both as to men and as to measures. Though it might therefore be allowable to suppose that the Executive could occasionally influence some individuals in the Senate, the supposition that he could in general purchase the integrity of the whole body would be strained and improbable. A man disposed to view human nature as it is, without either flattering its virtues or exaggerating its vices, will see sufficient ground of confidence in the probity of the Senate to rest satisfied not only that it will be impracticable for the Executive to corrupt or seduce a majority of its members, but that the necessity of its cooperation in the business of appointments will be a considerable and beneficial restraint on the conduct of that magistrate. Nor is the integrity of the Senate the only safeguard. The Constitution has provided some important guards against the danger of executive influence on the legislative body. It declares that "No senator or representative shall during the time for which he was elected, be appointed to any civil office under the United States, which shall have been created, or the emoluments whereof shall have been increased, during such time; and no person, holding any office under the United States, shall be a member of either house during his continuance in office."
